title: Ashtpadi 19, salok: nothing goes along
hook: nothing goes with you except devotion (Sukhmani 19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Panj Pyare: the Guru who took amrit from his own students, care and service running both ways. Today Sukhmani enters its last stretch, ashtpadis nineteen to twenty-four.

Anyone who has cleared out a parent's home knows the feeling. The drawers of rubber bands. The good china used twice. The boxes of papers that once mattered terribly: tax forms, warranties, letters. A lifetime of things, and every last bit of it stayed behind. You stand in the half-empty room holding a coffee mug and realize the person isn't in any of it. The salok of the nineteenth ashtpadi says this out loud, and then says what isn't left behind.
screen: `CLEARING OUT A PARENT'S HOME.` → `A LIFETIME OF THINGS, ALL LEFT.` → `THE PERSON ISN'T IN ANY OF IT.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: nothing goes along with you except devotion; all the poison of worldly things is ash. Earn the Name of the Lord; Nanak, this is the excellent wealth. Three words open it. Saath: with, alongside. Na chaalai: does not go. Bin bhajan: except devotion, the singing and remembering of God. So the first line is a short inventory: everything you own, and next to almost every item, does not go. Then the strong image: bikhiaa saglee chhaar. Bikhiaa is a word Gurbani uses for maya's poison, the pull of worldly things. Chhaar is ash. Not evil, exactly. Ash: what's left when the fire has burned out. The house, the car, the savings account aren't wicked. They're ash-in-waiting. Then the turn, and it's a money word. Kamaavanaa: to earn. Earn the Name. The salok doesn't tell you to stop earning; Sikhs are expected to work honestly and provide for their families. It tells you what else to earn, and it calls the Name dhan, wealth, and saar, the excellent, the essential. So this isn't a hymn against wealth. It's a hymn about which wealth travels. Over the next days the ashtpadi looks at what stays behind and what goes along. Today, only the inventory. And the salok makes no threat. It points at the room full of things and says: none of this comes with you, except the devotion.
screen: `SAATH NA CHAALAI: DOES NOT GO ALONG.` · `BIKHIAA IS ASH: CHHAAR.` · `KAMAAVANAA: EARN THE NAME.` · `WHICH WEALTH TRAVELS?` · then, large: `NOTHING GOES ALONG.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes move slowly around the room, the furniture, the phone, the clothes, the books, and to each thing say silently, without sadness, just accurately: this stays. Then close your eyes and ask what, if anything, is going along with you, and let the question sit unanswered.
Saath, with or alongside: its salok says saath na chaalai bin bhajan, nothing goes along except devotion; earn the Name, the excellent wealth.
Your line: nothing goes along. The things are ash-in-waiting; the Name is the wealth that travels. That's day five hundred ten.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the nineteenth ashtpadi with the salok saath na chaalai bin bhajan, and Sikh life pairs honest earning with remembering the Name as the wealth that lasts.

chat.who: your cousin, clearing out a closet
chat.says: Does that salok mean money and owning things are bad?
options: No; it calls things ash, not evil, and says earn the Name too: the wealth that goes along.
Yes; it tells Sikhs to stop earning and give up their houses, since all of it is poison.
No; it says your savings come with you, as long as you earned them honestly enough.
chat.meaning: The salok says nothing goes along except devotion, calls worldly things ash, and calls the earned Name the excellent wealth. Sikhs are expected to work honestly.

bhajan.meaning: devotion, the singing and remembering of God
